# Automated releases

Pushing a version tag runs `.github/workflows/release.yml`, generated by
**cargo-dist 0.33.0** from `dist-workspace.toml`. Do not edit the generated
workflow directly; edit the configuration or reusable workflows, then run
`dist generate`.

## What a release produces

| Platform | Architecture | Artifacts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux | x64 | `.tar.gz`, `.deb`, `.rpm`, `.pkg.tar.zst` |
| macOS | Apple Silicon and Intel | `.tar.gz` for each architecture |
| Windows | x64 | `.zip` |

Every binary archive and Linux package contains both `ario` and `ario_daemon`.
Archives include the license, README, and `man/` directory. Linux packages and
Homebrew install the `ario(1)` and `ario_daemon(1)` manual pages.
The release includes SHA-256 checksums,
the Homebrew formula, a source archive, and the cargo-dist manifest. Linux
packages have a separate `linux-packages.sha256` checksum file.

Linux binaries are built on Ubuntu 22.04 and require glibc 2.35 or newer.
The Linux packages declare aria2, CA certificates, glibc, and the GCC runtime
dependencies using each distribution's package names. `apt install ./file.deb`,
`dnf install ./file.rpm`, and `pacman -U ./file.pkg.tar.zst` resolve these
dependencies from the user's configured repositories. No apt, dnf, or pacman
repository is hosted by this pipeline.

The Arch package is named **ario-download-bin**. It conflicts with Arch's
unrelated `ario` MPD client because both install `/usr/bin/ario`; it does not
provide or replace the music player. Its installed commands are still `ario`
and `ario_daemon`.

macOS builds and native tests use `macos-15` for Apple Silicon and
`macos-15-intel` for Intel, explicitly selected in `dist-workspace.toml`.
These overrides avoid cargo-dist's default macOS 14 runners, which retire on
November 2, 2026.

Stable releases automatically update `Formula/ario.rb` in
[`peymanAzad/homebrew-tap`](https://github.com/peymanAzad/homebrew-tap).
The formula installs both binaries and depends on Homebrew's `aria2` package.
Users can then run:

```sh
brew install peymanAzad/tap/ario
brew upgrade ario
```

WinGet update submissions are optional until the first version has been
accepted by Microsoft. See the setup below.

## One-time Homebrew setup

1. Keep `peymanAzad/homebrew-tap` public and initialize it with a README so it
   has a default branch. The release pipeline creates the formula directory.
2. Create a fine-grained GitHub personal access token owned by `peymanAzad`,
   limited to **homebrew-tap**, with **Contents: Read and write** permission.
   The tap's default branch must allow this token to push formula updates.
3. In the **Ario repository**, open **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions**
   and create the repository secret **`HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN`** with that token.

The built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` creates releases in Ario. It cannot write to the
separate tap repository; that is why the additional secret is needed.
No token belongs in a source file, workflow literal, or chat message.

## One-time WinGet setup

Each stable release includes `ario-winget-manifests.tar.gz`, prepared from the
actual Windows ZIP. It contains the three manifests for `peymanAzad.Ario`,
including both portable executables, their archive checksum, and an
`aria2.aria2` package dependency. The executable paths are read from the ZIP.

After publishing the first stable release:

1. Download and extract `ario-winget-manifests.tar.gz` on Windows. Review the
   package metadata and publisher identity before submission.
2. Validate and install the local manifest, with WinGet's local manifest support
   enabled, then launch `ario` and verify that its daemon and aria2 start:

   ```powershell
   winget settings --enable LocalManifestFiles
   winget validate --manifest .\manifests\p\peymanAzad\Ario\0.1.0
   winget install --manifest .\manifests\p\peymanAzad\Ario\0.1.0
   ```

   Substitute the released version for `0.1.0`. Enabling local manifests may
   require an administrator terminal.
3. Submit the manifest directory to
   [`microsoft/winget-pkgs`](https://github.com/microsoft/winget-pkgs) following
   [Microsoft's submission process](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/package-manager/package/repository).
   Availability in the catalog depends on Microsoft's checks and review.
4. After acceptance, create a GitHub token for WingetCreate following
   [Microsoft's token instructions](https://aka.ms/winget-create-token) and
   store it in Ario's Actions repository secret **`WINGET_TOKEN`**.
5. Add the Actions repository **variable** **`WINGET_PACKAGE_ID`**, set to the
   accepted identifier, normally `peymanAzad.Ario`. Leave this variable unset
   until the initial package is accepted and the token is configured.

Subsequent stable releases invoke **WingetCreate 1.12.13.0** to update the
existing manifest and submit a PR. Submission does not guarantee immediate
catalog availability. The workflow skips prereleases.

If Microsoft's review requires a different identifier or installer structure,
adjust `scripts/winget-manifests.py` and set the accepted package ID before
enabling updates. WingetCreate updates the accepted upstream manifest rather
than replacing its reviewed settings with the bootstrap template.

## Preparing a release

Use this checklist for every release. The commands below use **0.2.3** as an
example; substitute the version being released throughout.

- [ ] **Finish and commit the intended changes.** Review the diff and confirm
  that the release includes the fixes or features you want to ship. Write a
  short user-facing summary of changes, compatibility requirements, and any
  migration steps for the release notes.
- [ ] **Choose an unused version.** Use a patch increment for compatible bug
  fixes, such as `0.2.2` → `0.2.3`. Fetch tags and confirm the proposed tag is
  absent:

  ```sh
  git fetch origin --tags
  git tag --list v0.2.3
  ```

  The second command must print nothing. Also check GitHub Releases for an
  existing release or draft using that version.
- [ ] **Update both Cargo files.** Change the package's `version` in
  `Cargo.toml`, then run:

  ```sh
  cargo check
  git diff -- Cargo.toml Cargo.lock
  git add Cargo.toml Cargo.lock
  git commit -m "Release v0.2.3"
  ```

  Verify that the `ario` entry in `Cargo.lock` has the new version. Other
  packages have their own versions; do not replace matching version strings
  throughout the lockfile.
- [ ] **Run the release checks from a clean working tree.** Install the pinned
  cargo-dist version using the maintenance instructions below if needed:

  ```sh
  git status --short
  cargo fmt --all --check
  cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings
  cargo test --locked --all-targets --no-fail-fast
  cargo package --locked
  dist generate --check
  dist plan --tag v0.2.3
  ```

  `git status --short` should print nothing, and every check must pass. If a
  check requires changes, commit those changes and repeat the affected checks.
- [ ] **Push the release branch, open a pull request, and wait for CI.** The
  **Release** PR checks build archives and Linux packages without publishing.
  They test all four release targets; Linux also checks formatting, Clippy,
  and Cargo packaging. Debian and Arch installation smoke checks verify that
  the packaged daemon starts aria2, serves `/health`, and shuts down. Merge
  only after the required checks pass.
- [ ] **Tag the merged release commit and push that tag.** Update your local
  `master`, verify that its package version and release changes are correct,
  and confirm the working tree is clean before tagging:

  ```sh
  git switch master
  git pull --ff-only origin master
  git status --short
  git log -1 --oneline
  git tag -a v0.2.3 -m "Ario v0.2.3"
  git push origin v0.2.3
  ```

  The tag version must match `Cargo.toml` and the `ario` entry in `Cargo.lock`.
  Pushing this tag starts publication. The workflow creates the GitHub release
  after builds and Linux packaging succeed; leave release creation to it.
- [ ] **Wait for the entire Release workflow.** Confirm GitHub publication,
  Homebrew publishing, and the WinGet submission job if enabled. Review the
  published assets and checksums for all supported platforms. Add your
  user-facing change summary to the generated release notes, retaining their
  installation and download information.
- [ ] **Publish the Cargo package.** The GitHub release workflow does **not**
  publish to crates.io. To make this version available through
  `cargo install ario --locked`, run these commands from the clean tagged
  release commit, using your crates.io publishing credentials:

  ```sh
  cargo publish --locked --dry-run
  cargo publish --locked
  ```

  Confirm that crates.io lists the intended version. Skip this step for
  releases you intentionally do not distribute through Cargo.
- [ ] **Verify the installed release.** Install or upgrade using the published
  packages or archives, confirm both `ario` and `ario_daemon` are installed,
  and restart the daemon to use the new binary. Launch Ario, download a small
  file, and exercise the behavior changed in this release. For the clipboard
  concurrency fix, import several links with a queue limit of one and verify
  that one transfers at a time and the next starts automatically. Check
  Homebrew on macOS and Windows installation on Windows when available;
  record any platform checks you could not perform.

Prerelease versions such as `0.2.0-beta.1` must also be recorded in Cargo.toml
and Cargo.lock before pushing their tags. They produce GitHub prereleases and
Linux packages, while leaving the stable Homebrew formula and WinGet catalog
unchanged. Arch prerelease versions use an alphabetic suffix (for example,
`0.2.0pre.beta.1-1`) so pacman orders them below the final `0.2.0-1` package.
Use plain `major.minor.patch` versions for stable releases.

After the first stable release, verify Homebrew installation on macOS and
installation of all three Linux package formats. Windows and macOS installation
checks still require those platforms; a Linux development machine cannot
confirm their end-to-end behavior.

## Local checks and maintenance

Install the pinned release tool:

```sh
cargo install cargo-dist --locked --version 0.33.0
dist generate --check
dist plan --tag v0.1.0
dist build --artifacts=local --target=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
```

With nFPM 2.47.0 installed, build Linux packages from that archive:

```sh
bash scripts/package-linux.sh 0.1.0 \
  target/distrib/ario-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz target/linux-packages
```

The script produces all three Linux package formats and their checksums.

Packages intended for distribution must use the CI-built binaries. Local
builds on newer systems can require a newer glibc than the declared baseline.
The dependency floors in `packaging/nfpm.yaml` and `packaging/nfpm-arch.yaml`
must be updated together with the Linux runner if the baseline changes.

After changing the dist configuration or `.github/release-build-setup.yml`,
run `dist generate` and commit the generated workflow as well. Pin updates to
cargo-dist and nFPM deliberately; update the nFPM archive checksum when changing
its version. If available, run `actionlint` against the workflows.

If a release fails before publication, fix the failure and rerun failed jobs.
If Homebrew publishing fails after the GitHub release is live, run **Publish
Homebrew formula** from the Actions tab on the default branch and enter the
published tag, for example `v0.2.2`. The workflow downloads `ario.rb` from that
release, adds the formula test, checks its style, and updates the tap if the
formula changed. Use the tag you want users to install from the tap.

If only WinGet publishing fails, repair its credentials or settings and rerun
that failed job. Published versions and their tags should remain immutable.
